title: Judge blasts prosecutors, refuses to sign new criminal complaint against ex-FBI officials
description: Deputy Assistant Director for Counterterrorism at the FBI Nikki Floris, testifies before the House Judiciary Committee hearing on Capitol Hill in Wash
body: Deputy Assistant Director for Counterterrorism at the FBI Nikki Floris, testifies before the House Judiciary Committee hearing on Capitol Hill in Washington, Oct. 22, 2019.Susan Walsh | APA judge on Tuesday sharply criticized federal prosecutors for failing to get judicial approval before filing a new criminal complaint overnight against two ex-FBI officials accused of lying to Congress about investigations of Hunter Biden.Magistrate Judge Zia Faruqui said he would not sign off on the new complaint, which added a charge of obstruction against Nikki Floris and Bradley Benavides in U.S. District Court in Washington."I am not going to bless it as a superseding complaint," Faruqui said at a court hearing, after Floris' lawyers filed a motion arguing the new complaint was legally deficient and filed in bad faith.He told prosecutors that if they wanted to file a superseding complaint, a judge first would have to find probable cause that a crime had been committed, instead of sending him the complaint in the middle of the night and expecting him to sign it.Faruqui said he did not believe that federal prosecutors had previously sought to file a criminal complaint without a judge's signature."It is not our court's practice … that unsigned complaints are filed in the docket," Faruqui said."I'm concerned with your view as to what the law is," the judge told the prosecutors. "Why today, on this one case, have you changed the entire history of how you charge cases?"The superseding complaint that prosecutors in the office of D.C. U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro filed in court early Tuesday contained a signature block with Faruqui's name typed out. But the judge had not personally signed the complaint.It was filed hours before prosecutors and defense lawyers were due to appear before Faruqui for a preliminary hearing on the original complaint.That first complaint, made public last Friday, accuses Floris and Benavides of making false statements to the House Judiciary Committee in 2023 about their involvement in investigations of Hunter Biden, the son of former President Joe Biden. Floris and Benavides were arrested Friday and have been released.The new complaint sought to charge them with obstruction and attempted obstruction of a congressional proceeding.Typically, criminal cases for conduct that occurred well in the past — as this one alleges — are lodged through an indictment, not a criminal complaint. To obtain an indictment, prosecutors must present evidence to a grand jury, which then determines whether the evidence is sufficient to charge a defendant.A criminal complaint only requires a judge's signature. It is often used to obtain an arrest warrant in situations where prosecutors need to move quickly.At Tuesday's hearing, Faruqui homed in on the way prosecutors filed charges."This case was charged by criminal complaint on Oct. 20, for testimony that occurred over a period of time in 2023," he said. "As I noted, and I think it continues to be the case, that it's unusual in a case that has conduct like this to be charged by criminal complaint.""This has to get to a grand jury," Faruqui said. Under federal rules, prosecutors generally must obtain an indictment within 30 days of a person's arrest, or risk the case being dismissed.Floris' lawyers, in an emailed statement to CNBC on Tuesday morning, criticized the prosecutors' conduct."In the middle of the night, the government filed an unsigned and unsworn complaint attempting to fix the issues with their original charge against Ms. Floris and adding a new charge just as meritless as the first one," the attorneys wrote."In our combined decades of DOJ service, we have never seen or even heard of something like this being filed. That's because the public lodging of criminal charges must be authorized by the grand jury, a judge, or the defendant herself," they wrote. "Here, the government has taken that power for itself in a desperate attempt to delay our client's right to challenge the charges in court and litigate this case in the media, rather than the courtroom," they said."We have asked to address this outrageous government conduct against a decorated public servant at today's court hearing," Floris' legal team wrote.In their motion to strike the superseding criminal complaint, the lawyers argued the document "represents a serious abuse of the criminal charging process, a troubling disregard for the judicial safeguards governing the initiation of criminal proceedings, and a calculated effort to evade judicial scrutiny and shield the government's allegations from adversarial testing at the scheduled preliminary hearing."

schema.headline: Judge blasts prosecutors, refuses to sign new criminal complaint against ex-FBI officials

title: Honda warns 50% Canada auto tariffs would be catastrophic for industry
description: An American flag flutters outside a Honda automobile dealership in Irvine, California, U.S., March 27, 2025. Mike Blake | ReutersDETROIT — The automot
body: An American flag flutters outside a Honda automobile dealership in Irvine, California, U.S., March 27, 2025. Mike Blake | ReutersDETROIT — The automotive industry faces a "catastrophic" scenario if the U.S. and Canada cannot reach a new trade deal by the end of this year, an executive with Honda Motor warned Tuesday. President Donald Trump has threatened to double tariffs on Canadian vehicles and parts from 25% to 50% on Jan. 1 if the two countries don't reach a deal."That really would be catastrophic for the entire industry," Jennifer Thomas, senior vice president of corporate affairs at American Honda Motor Co., said during a Reuters automotive conference in Detroit.Thomas said, ideally, the countries would also include Mexico in the arrangement and reach a trilateral deal, like the United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement, or USMCA. Trade associations representing Honda, as well as every major player in the U.S. automotive industry, have been advocating for that more comprehensive accord and against bilateral arrangements between two countries.Her comments come months after U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer announced that the U.S. would not automatically extend the USMCA, moving the trade pact into an annual review process instead of a 16-year trilateral extension.Trump negotiated the USMCA to replace the North American Free Trade Agreement during his first term and it took effect in 2020. He later soured on it and accused Canada of "ripping off the United States of America for years."Thomas said she is "cautiously optimistic" that cooler heads will prevail to avoid the doubling of tariffs, which Trump threatened in August if no deal can be reached.She said she's encouraged by recent reports that the U.S. and Canada have reestablished trade talks, including easing levies on critical materials such as aluminum."Our message has been clear: We need that trilateral agreement to stay in place in order for the U.S. industry to be competitive," Thomas said. "It's integral to our success."Honda is the second-largest producer of vehicles in Canada behind Toyota Motor, but many automotive officials have voiced concerns about the lack of a North American trade deal and tariff uncertainty due to the number of parts that regularly cross the borders for vehicle production.While Honda has established large operations in Canada, the company reports that more than 60% of the vehicles it sells in the U.S. are manufactured domestically across multiple U.S. assembly plants."I never thought I would see the North American region be put at a disadvantage like this," Thomas said, adding that some overseas countries have better tariff rates.The Trump administration has negotiated trade deals with other countries such as Japan and South Korea, which are major exporters of vehicles to the U.S., that include 15% tariffs on vehicles.

schema.headline: Honda warns 50% Canada auto tariffs would be catastrophic for industry

title: Grand jury rejects DOJ bid to indict ex-Trump WH aide Cassidy Hutchinson: Reports
description: Cassidy Hutchinson, who was an aide to former White House Chief of Staff Mark Meadows during the administration of former U.S. President Donald Trump,
body: Cassidy Hutchinson, who was an aide to former White House Chief of Staff Mark Meadows during the administration of former U.S. President Donald Trump, testifies during a public hearing of the U.S. House Select Committee to investigate the January 6 Attack on the U.S. Capitol, on Capitol Hill in Washington, June 28, 2022.Evelyn Hockstein | ReutersA federal grand jury in Washington, D.C., rejected a request by the Department of Justice to indict former White House aide Cassidy Hutchinson in connection with her congressional testimony about President Donald Trump's conduct during the Jan. 6, 2021, mob attack on the U.S. Capitol, The Washington Post reported Tuesday.Prosecutors in the DOJ's Civil Rights Division sought to charge Hutchinson with a crime based on claims she made false statements, MS NOW said, citing two people with knowledge of the case.Senior DOJ lawyer Neville Hedley told Magistrate Judge Zia Faruqui in open court on Tuesday afternoon that the grand jury had rejected the requested indictment without naming Hutchinson as the target, according to The Post.It is extremely rare for a grand jury to refuse to indict when prosecutors present evidence of alleged crimes. But federal prosecutors in Washington, since Trump took office again in January 2025, have several times failed to obtain a grand jury indictment they sought.In recent weeks, prosecutors have filed separate criminal cases in U.S. District Court in D.C. against former FBI Director James Comey, and two former FBI officials with charging documents that are not grand jury indictments. In both cases, the alleged conduct occurred years earlier. Typically, in such cases, prosecutors would seek a grand jury indictment.The DOJ used a document known as an "information" to charge him on Oct. 5 with retaining or sharing national defense information with someone not authorized to possess it.Comey's lawyers accused the DOJ of using the method in an effort to suspend the charge's 10-year statute of limitations. The lawyers have asked a judge to dismiss the case, saying the deadline for obtaining a grand jury indictment was on Oct. 5, the day the information was filed.Hutchinson testified in June 2022 to the House Select Committee that investigated the Jan. 6 Capitol riot by a mob of Trump supporters, whose attack delayed for hours the confirmation of Joe Biden's electoral victory in the 2020 election.She said that after Trump spoke at a rally outside the White House that preceded the attack, then-White House official Tony Ornato asked her, "Did you effing hear what happened in [the president's vehicle,] The Beast?"She testified that Ornato told her that when Trump got in the car, he was under the impression from his then-Chief of Staff Mark Meadows that they going to the Capitol, as he had claimed in his speech to supporters at the rally.When Robert Engel, the head of Trump's security detail, said the president could not go there because the area was not secure, Trump "had a very strong, a very angry response to that," Hutchinson testified that Ornato said."Tony described him as being irate," Hutchinson said, noting that Trump had said something like: "I'm the effing president, take me up to the Capitol now," according to Ornato.When Engel refused again to drive him to the Capitol, Trump "reached up towards the front of the vehicle to grab at the steering wheel. Mr. Engel grabbed his arm, said, 'Sir, you need to take your hand off the steering wheel. We're going back to the West Wing,'" Hutchinson testified.Trump "then used his free hand to lunge toward Bobby Engel," Hutchinson said she was told by Ornato. This is breaking news. Please refresh for updates.

title: As holiday shopping approaches, seasonal hiring gives 'mixed signals,' experts say
description: On Oct. 20, Amazon said it plans to employ more than 300,000 full-time, part-time and seasonal workers ahead of the peak shopping period, according to
body: On Oct. 20, Amazon said it plans to employ more than 300,000 full-time, part-time and seasonal workers ahead of the peak shopping period, according to a press release. In 2025, Amazon pledged 250,000 holiday jobs, marking a 20% increase in jobs.UPS, one of the largest U.S. shipping companies, announced on Oct. 7 it would hire 100,000 seasonal employees in 2026, down nearly 10% from the company's 2025 holiday hiring target.These announcements, together with fewer retailers providing recruitment headcounts ahead of the holidays are part of why experts say seasonal hiring is giving them "mixed signals," says Andy Challenger, chief revenue officer of outplacement firm Challenger, Gray & Christmas."I don't expect this to be an explosive seasonal hiring year like we saw in '21 and '22," Challenger tells CNBC Make It. Following Amazon's announcement, Challenger says "there's reason to be a little bit more positive than we originally thought."Seasonal job postings as of Sept. 30, 2026 surpassed 2025 levels during the same period, according to an Oct. 15 report from Indeed Hiring Lab, the job board's economic research wing. Experts say non-retail jobs are driving the growth.Indeed's report found that seasonal hiring in 2026, as measured by the number of job postings, is up 10% from 2025. Researchers scrubbed Indeed and other job boards for seasonal jobs, which they define as roles with at least one holiday-related descriptor in the title. Indeed director of economic research Laura Ullrich tells CNBC Make It that the data reflects "a large percentage of jobs" — even those whose companies did not pay Indeed to upload their openings on the site.While many retailers have been silent about their seasonal hiring plans, "We've seen some positive additions," Challenger said of Amazon's hiring plans. "We did see UPS is down a little bit. Exporting goods is down a little bit."The new retail seasonal hiring strategyRetail has long dominated seasonal hiring, but its stronghold has faltered. In 2019, jobs in retail accounted for around 66% of all seasonal roles, according to Indeed. Today, retail adds 61% of all seasonal work opportunities. Loading and stocking roles, which accounted for 3.5% of seasonal hiring posts in 2019, now represent 9% of all holiday job listings as of Sept. 30, 2026. The warehouse category is the fastest-growing among retail, sales, customer service, transportation and food preparation, according to Indeed. As for individual roles, the five most in-demand, non-retail titles include customer service representative, unloader, delivery driver, photographer and stocker, the Indeed report found.Experts at Indeed say the shift in seasonal hiring reflects how e-commerce has reshaped holiday shopping. The share of Americans who shop online is up to 87%, according to data from the Statista Research Department, and experts forecast e-commerce retail sales growth of 6% every year until 2030.Bain & Company projects a $1 trillion breakthrough in holiday retail sales across the U.S. in 2026, a historic first boosted by inflation. Challenger says the figure "doesn't necessarily mean more sales or more revenue or profit."Instead, the forecast shows that while the high cost of necessities like food and gas are changing consumer habits, inflation "hasn't totally dampened consumers' expectations of participating in shopping this holiday season," Challenger explains.To prepare for the holiday season, retailers are posting more permanent part-time jobs in place of seasonal roles, says Ullrich. Non-seasonal, part-time roles accounted for 38% of retail jobs in September 2025, and today make up 49% of the holiday retail job market. Seasonal roles accounted for just 20% of retailers' overall holiday job posts in September 2026, a decline from the same period in 2025.In response to sales forecasts, retailers have taken different approaches to seasonal hiring. Spirit Halloween said it would hire 52,000 employees on June 11 and Michaels plans to onboard over 10,000 workers for the holidays. Per Target's website, the company said it would lean on its existing workforce before looking for seasonal hires. The big-box store did not announce headcounts.Ullrich sees the trend to hire more permanent employees across retail "as a positive" and says retailers "realize they need more employees on a permanent basis."More people are searching for seasonal jobsSeasonal work is also in high demand for job seekers. Desktop searches for seasonal and holiday terms are up 28% in 2026 against 2025 search data on Indeed, a sign that workers hope to earn extra cash before the year concludes.An Indeed report from June 9 found that 16% of active job seekers already hold multiple jobs. On average, workers with multiple jobs tripled their application volume in the month leading up to landing their second role. Workers with service jobs, characterized by high turnover rates and inconsistent scheduling, are the most likely to hold another job. Among active job seekers, Food preparation workers make up the largest share, 17%, looking for additional employment.

schema.headline: As holiday shopping approaches, seasonal hiring gives 'mixed signals,' experts say

title: Oracle integrates ChatGPT, Codex into apps and expands cloud chip lineup
description: Oracle on Tuesday announced an expanded collaboration with OpenAI that brings the artificial intelligence lab's ChatGPT and Codex into the software ma
body: Oracle on Tuesday announced an expanded collaboration with OpenAI that brings the artificial intelligence lab's ChatGPT and Codex into the software maker's applications to make databases more actionable.Mahesh Thiagarajan, Oracle's president of Cloud Infrastructure, told CNBC at Oracle AI World in Las Vegas that using ChatGPT "allows anybody to build an application, deploy it, manage it."OpenAI CEO Sam Altman is set to join Oracle co-CEO Clay Magouyrk on stage for an Oracle AI World keynote on Tuesday at 12:40 p.m. ET.For OpenAI, the announcement represents another example of the frontier lab's push into the enterprise market, just one day after its key competitor, Anthropic, filed its S-1 as it heads toward an initial public offering.Oracle's database plays a crucial role in underpinning businesses across healthcare and finance in logging and securing data.OpenAI CEO Sam Altman speaking at Oracle AI World in Las Vegas on Oct. 27, 2026.CNBCThiagarajan said his team observed OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra model get trained at Oracle's Stargate data center campus in Abilene, Texas, and could see the real-time benefits."More businesses are choosing OpenAI as we make it easier to put AI to work through the tools and systems they already use," said Greg Brockman, president and co-founder of OpenAI, in the press release.Oracle also said Tuesday that it is making different hardware accessible on its cloud infrastructure, including Google's tensor processing unit AI chips and OpenAI's Jalapeño chip."Now customers can actually have infinite possibilities in terms of how they can drive AI," Thiagarajan said.It is the first time Google's custom chips will run on another hyperscaler's cloud, and illustrates how the companies are increasingly looking for opportunities to get their hardware in the hands of the frontier labs.Thiagarajan added that the scarcity of chips remains an ongoing issue and that customers such as OpenAI can benefit from having different accelerators to choose from. When asked whether this marks a pivot away from Nvidia GPUs, Thiagarajan said no, adding that Nvidia chips are "the best, most fungible," and that the AI market remains incredibly large.OpenAI's Jalapeño chip and Cerebras will also run on Oracle Cloud Infrastructure. The Cerebras deal is material, but the AI chipmaker won't be disclosing the scale because it's in a quiet period, a Cerebras spokesperson said.Cerebras stock climbed about 8% following the news. Oracle shares were up nearly 5% on Tuesday.Read more CNBC tech newsA guide to some of the biggest risks in Anthropic's IPO prospectusNvidia, AMD to invest $4 billion in Meta as tech giants deepen AI partnershipApple responds to user reports of broken iPhone Duo screens on new foldable phoneAnthropic's IPO plans: 900% revenue retention, but $80 billion in first-half lossesThe announcement comes seven months after market-leading cloud Amazon Web Services announced plans to bring Cerebras hardware into its data centers, a major point of validation.Thiagarajan also addressed Oracle's multibillion New Mexico data center dubbed Project Jupiter and the ongoing pushback it's receiving from the local community. He said Jupiter represents just one of the 30-40 different data center projects in development, per quarter, for the company."We're actually not too worried about what we're doing because I think we're building global infrastructure," he said.A hearing to address air quality permitting is scheduled for Dec. 7 in Sunland Park, where the controversial data center has already broken ground. The political pushback tied to the project prompted Oracle to deliver a force majeure notice to its backer Blue Owl Capital last month. Right now, Oracle maintains that the project is on schedule.Investors are now counting down to Oracle's investor day, where investors will want to see if the company can back its fiscal year 2030 revenue targets and if the margin profile of its cloud deals has changed due to the rising cost of capital.Bank of America analysts wrote to clients that updates on Oracle's major data center projects are among the topics they expect clarity on at the meeting.Oracle shares are down more than 30% this year due in part to concerns about how the company plans to finance its ambitious digital infrastructure pipeline.— CNBC's Jordan Novet contributed to this articleStock Chart IconStock chart iconOracle stock chart.watch now

schema.headline: Oracle integrates ChatGPT, Codex into apps and expands cloud chip lineup

title: Jim Cramer warns investors not to get fooled by the latest AI stock rally
description: Monday - Friday, 6:00 - 7:00 PM ETMad MoneyPublished Tue, Oct 27 20266:24 PM EDTKey PointsCNBC’s Jim Cramer warned that the latest rally in AI stocks
body: Monday - Friday, 6:00 - 7:00 PM ETMad MoneyPublished Tue, Oct 27 20266:24 PM EDTKey PointsCNBC’s Jim Cramer warned that the latest rally in AI stocks doesn't mean the data center trade is out of the woods.Cramer pointed to three lingering risks.CNBC's Jim Cramer warned Tuesday that investors may be getting ahead of themselves by declaring the artificial intelligence trade back on track.AI-related stocks rallied for a second straight session, fueled by renewed enthusiasm for chipmakers after a group of banks and Blackstone announced $63 billion in financing for Anthropic to purchase Broadcom's computing hardware. The gains followed Monday's rally, sparked in part by Anthropic's S-1 filing. But Cramer cautioned the renewed optimism doesn't resolve the pressures facing the data center trade, which was hit hard late last week. "I'm pleased that people feel so comfortable that tech is all good to go because there is money flowing back in," the "Mad Money" host said. "I don't think that's a reason to call all clear. I think it's a reason to look at other sectors in the economy."Cramer's skepticism centers on three lingering risks.First, Cramer remains concerned about smaller AI infrastructure companies, known as neoclouds, that are taking on significant debt to fund the data center build-out. Rising interest rates have intensified worries about their ability to sustain those borrowing costs. Cramer singled out CoreWeave, whose bonds have yielded as much as 15%, along with Nebius and Iren. Despite an almost 8% rebound in CoreWeave shares Tuesday, he warned that fresh negativity around CoreWeave could emerge. "I have learned that after every positive story about anything in the data center, there will be a plethora of negative stories about something wrong, including Coreweave," Cramer said.Second, Cramer questioned whether the Broadcom-Anthropic financing deal was as reassuring as investors believed. While the $63 billion package demonstrated that lenders were still willing to finance massive AI investments, Cramer raised concerns that Anthropic is borrowing money to buy Broadcom's technology, rather than paying for it with profits from its own business. "People don't seem to grasp that [Anthropic] got the money in the Broadcom-arranged financing deal to purchase equipment from Broadcom," he said.Finally, Cramer said that Tuesday's calmer bond market could prove short-lived. Oil prices declined and the 10-year Treasury yield fell below 5%, easing some pressure on AI companies that need to borrow heavily to fund their data center investments. But those conditions could reverse, particularly with the Federal Reserve set to announce its latest interest rate decision Wednesday afternoon, followed by Chairman Kevin Warsh's post-meeting press conference. The midterm elections next week and potential flare-ups in the Middle East may represent additional sources of volatility. "With the exception of Nvidia, these data center companies don't have a lot of money. So they have to borrow the money," Cramer said. "The rates are getting so high that the return is getting uncertain. That hasn't changed at all."Cramer emphasized that he remains "an unabashed believer in the AI build-out." But until the industry's financing challenges ease, he isn't ready to declare the coast clear.

schema.headline: Jim Cramer warns investors not to get fooled by the latest AI stock rally

title: Anthropic's IPO is risky business
description: CEO of Anthropic Dario Amodei looks on as U.S. President Donald Trump holds a press briefing with AI executives following a meeting on artificial inte
body: CEO of Anthropic Dario Amodei looks on as U.S. President Donald Trump holds a press briefing with AI executives following a meeting on artificial intelligence, outside the West Wing of the White House on September 29, 2026 in Washington, DC. Kevin Dietsch | Getty ImagesAnthropic's much-anticipated initial public offering is giving potential investors some perspective on the risky business of artificial intelligence.More than 90 pages of Anthropic's IPO prospectus, revealed Monday, center on the AI lab's multitude of corporate risk factors, many of which go beyond the kinds of boilerplate scenarios typically found in  corporate filings.From the end of humanity to the company's current clash with the Trump administration, Anthropic's IPO document underscores how one of the most well-capitalized startups in history foresees the future of its operations.Anthropic's IPO gets existentialThe Claude maker's risks include a laundry list of ways its models can cause harm, including potentially  "catastrophic or existential risks to humanity." It's imperative for Anthropic to emphasize AI safety because failure to do so could adversely affect its "brand, business, financial condition, and results of operations," the filing said. But fierce competition, market pressure and stakeholder expectations make the task of safely developing and implementing bleeding-edge foundation models particularly challenging.Anthropic can't guarantee that its AI safety efforts will be adequate, as the technology's inherent complexity makes it difficult for the company to plan for and predict every potential scenario.Feeling the data center heat The public's souring position on data centers poses a major risk for Anthropic, which relies on an ever-expanding portfolio of state-of-the-art computing facilities to train and maintain its prized foundation models.And with the midterm elections approaching, the tech industry's massive data center build-out has turned political, with lawmakers in 16 states considering moratoriums, according to the National Conference of State Legislatures."Opposition to data center development  has also become more organized and coordinated across jurisdictions and our public profile may draw particular attention to projects associated with us," the filing said.Power problemsAnthropic's future success depends not only on building giant data centers, but also on the electrical and related power infrastructure needed to juice those computing facilities.The lack of "sufficient electrical power" across the nation and world poses big risks to Anthropic and its rivals, the filing notes. Even if energy becomes more readily available through "on-site natural gas-fired generation," that power could become more expensive with so much demand, the filing said.The kids are not alrightRivals like OpenAI and Meta have come under fire from lawmakers and plaintiffs' attorneys over allegations that the design and implementation of their AI models and apps have fostered certain child safety-related harms. Meta recently agreed to pay roughly $17 billion in a settlement with multiple state attorneys general in litigation involving child mental health and technology addiction.Thus far, Anthropic has largely avoided scrutiny, but the filing noted that the company could potentially face its own legal headaches. Based on its terms of service, minors aren't allowed to access Claude and related products.Anthropic knows it has work to do protecting children "as adoption of our models grows, including by minors and other vulnerable users, notwithstanding our efforts to restrict such access."No slowpokesThe company calling to pace the frontier also says it's a risk to move too slowly. Anthropic needs to keep racing and needs the rest of the business world to keep up. If companies curb their AI spending, Anthropic could feel the burn. "If the market for our models, platform, and applications develops more slowly than we expect or declines, our growth may slow or stall, and our business, financial condition, and results of operations could be adversely affected," the filing says.The prospectus also cites reduced demand for frontier models as a risk. Customers might find that lower-cost models work fine for them and that "incremental performance gains at the frontier do not justify the additional cost," instead choosing cheaper, or open-source alternatives.WATCH: Anthropic IPO filing shows what's happening on demand side of AI trade.watch now

title: Robinhood shares fall 4% as crypto slump weighs on profits, offsetting gains in new businesses
description: Omar Marques | Lightrocket | Getty ImagesRobinhood shares fell 4% in after-hours trading as investors digested weaker-than-expected third-quarter earn
body: Omar Marques | Lightrocket | Getty ImagesRobinhood shares fell 4% in after-hours trading as investors digested weaker-than-expected third-quarter earnings despite growth in options trading and prediction markets.Here's how the brokerage performed in its quarter ended Sept. 30,  compared with Wall Street estimates, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG: Earnings per share: 51 cents vs. 56 cents expectedRevenue: $1.42 billion vs. $1.42 billion expectedRobinhood's net income fell to $468 million, or 51 cents per share, from $556 million, or 61 cents per share, a year ago. Revenue represented a 12% increase from $1.27 billion in the same quarter last year.Despite that gain, transaction-based revenue of $867 million came in below Wall Street estimates from StreetAccount of $879 million, putting the focus on whether Robinhood can sustain momentum across its trading businesses and reduce its reliance on volatile market activity. Robinhood has been diversifying its business as it tries to expand its brokerage app into a broader financial services platform. Options trading and event contracts have become increasingly important sources of transaction revenue, while the company has continued to invest in wealth management, subscriptions and other offerings.Transaction-based revenue grew 19% from the same period last year to $867 million, driven primarily by a more than 500% increase in event contracts revenue. Additionally, options revenue grew 31% to $399 million and equities revenue rose 41% to $121 million. Those gains were partially offset by cryptocurrency revenue, which fell 55% to $120 million.Chief Financial Officer Shiv Verma told CNBC event contracts on crypto movements did well in the quarter, offering investors another way to express a view on crypto despite the slump in prices and spot trading.Net deposits on the Robinhood platform totaled $15.7 billion for the quarter, equal to a 17% annualized growth rate based on total platform assets at the end of Q2 2026. Over the past year, net deposits totaled $71 billion, representing 21% growth compared with total platform assets at the end of Q3 2025.—With reporting from CNBC's Robert Hum and Kate Rooney

schema.headline: Robinhood shares fall 4% as crypto slump weighs on profits, offsetting gains in new businesses

title: Margin debt growth slows sharply as stock market warning signs build
description: Traders work on the floor of the New York Stock Exchange (NYSE) in New York City.Jeenah Moon | ReutersThe pace at which investors are borrowing money
body: Traders work on the floor of the New York Stock Exchange (NYSE) in New York City.Jeenah Moon | ReutersThe pace at which investors are borrowing money to invest in stocks has cooled substantially, raising concern that the stock market may be due for a fall.Recent FINRA data shows the annual growth in margin debt fell to 31.4% in September from 53.7% in May, Bank of America technical strategist Paul Ciana pointed out in a Friday note. Ciana warned that slowing borrowing momentum from extreme levels has been associated with previous market peaks.May's growth rate in 2026 was the fourth highest since 1998, according to a BofA analysis. The three higher extremes took place in 2000, 2007 and 2021 — all of which preceded stock market declines.Earlier this year, borrowing was increasing much faster than stocks were rising. Analysts view high borrowing levels as a contrarian signal, similar to bull-bear sentiment indicators. At $1.48 trillion, margin debt in September is 1.5% below June's record of $1.5 trillion. High leverage can have snowball effects in a market downturn. Lower prices trigger demands for additional collateral or forced sales, which accelerate a downturn. Individual investors can be hit hard. Tesla investor Hy Luu, for example, refinanced his home to raise $30,000 to pay down margin debt during the stock's 2022 decline.BofA sees other market warning signs, including widening high-yield credit spreads and a rotation toward defensive sectors like healthcare and consumer staples.Paradoxically, the rotation into those sectors has pushed them to "bubble-risk levels," BofA's equity derivatives team said in a note on Tuesday. Similar shifts occurred in the late 1990s dot-com era and Covid rally, they added. "These dynamics provide further evidence that markets continue to move towards a more bubble-like state."The bull case is that the midterms could alleviate some of the market's uncertainty and trigger a relief rally, Ciana noted. "Typically, risk assets such as the S&P 500 rebound after midterms unless more severe downside risks materialize."

schema.headline: Margin debt growth slows sharply as stock market warning signs build

title: Coca-Cola hikes earnings outlook, even as it sees lackluster demand in North America
description: Multipacks of Coca-Cola Original Taste glass bottles, 4x200ml, line a supermarket shelf in Bari, Italy, on September 15, 2026. Matteo Della Torre | Nu
body: Multipacks of Coca-Cola Original Taste glass bottles, 4x200ml, line a supermarket shelf in Bari, Italy, on September 15, 2026. Matteo Della Torre | Nurphoto | Getty ImagesCoca-Cola on Tuesday raised its full-year outlook for the third straight quarter, despite lackluster demand in its home market.For the full year, Coke now expects comparable earnings per share to grow at least 11%, up from its prior forecast of an increase in the range of 9% to 10%. The beverage giant also anticipates that its organic revenue will climb at least 5%, a slight increase from its previous outlook of approximately 5% growth.CEO Henrique Braun attributed the company's strong results to its "speed and discipline" despite the "uneven environment," he said on the company's earnings conference call. Looking ahead to 2027, the company expects consumer behavior to remain unchanged, CFO John Murphy said. In recent quarters, Braun and other executives have said North American shoppers are under pressure, stretched thin by inflation and economic uncertainty, and looking for value. But the beverage giant has also said consumers are still buying its drinks, from premium brands like Fairlife to its namesake soda. Shares of the company fell less than 1% in morning trading on its gloomy forecast for the consumer environment.Here's what the company reported compared with what Wall Street analysts surveyed by LSEG were expecting: Earnings per share: 91 cents adjusted vs. 88 cents expectedRevenue: $13.4 billion vs. $12.92 billion expected Coke reported fiscal third-quarter net income attributable to shareholders of $4.01 billion, or 93 cents per share, up from $3.7 billion, or 86 cents per share, a year earlier.Excluding transaction gains and other items, Coke earned 91 cents per share.Net sales rose 7% to $13.4 billion. Coke's organic revenue, which strips out acquisitions, divestitures and foreign currency, also climbed 7% in the quarter.For the second straight quarter, the company's unit case volume increased 5%, helped by higher demand outside of North America. Coke's home market reported flat volume. However, the company's North American business would have reported volume growth if not for the timing of the Fourth of July holiday and the monthslong shortage of Topo Chico, a sparkling water brand Coke owns, Murphy told CNBC."The underlying momentum remains quite strong," he said. "Consumer sentiment is largely unchanged in the sense that, wherever you are on the income scale, you're looking for value, and I think our system here has done a good job interpreting that."In North America, Coke's at-home business is faring better than its away-from-home segment, which includes restaurants, movie theaters and amusement parks. The restaurant industry is still under pressure, and Coke expects that to continue through the rest of the year, Murphy told analysts on the company's earnings conference call.Globally, Coke's sparkling soft drinks business saw volume increase 5% during the quarter, lifted by growth of Coke, Coke Zero Sugar and Diet Coke. Diet Coke is having a "resurgence," Murphy told CNBC. Gen Z consumers in the U.S. have nicknamed it a "fridge cigarette," while consumers in India threw Diet Coke parties as shortages tied to the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran have made the drink scarce."It's a brand that's almost reinventing itself with the next generation of consumers," he said.Coke has also gained market share as rival PepsiCo sees its soda business struggle, according to Murphy. Still, some of Coke's soda brands, like Sprite, have "some work to do."Coke's water, sports, coffee and tea division also saw volume climb by 5%. Increased demand for its water, which includes its premium Smartwater brand, fueled the growth. Demand for its tea and coffee was flat, while sports drinks declined.The company's juice, value-added dairy and plant-based beverages business reported flat volume, despite growth in brands like Fairlife and Minute Maid.

schema.headline: Coca-Cola hikes earnings outlook, even as it sees lackluster demand in North America

title: Polymarket faces renewed CFTC probe over U.S. access to offshore platform
description: Shayne Coplan, chief executive officer of Polymarket, on the floor of the New York Stock Exchange (NYSE) in New York, US, on Thursday, Nov. 13, 2025.
body: Shayne Coplan, chief executive officer of Polymarket, on the floor of the New York Stock Exchange (NYSE) in New York, US, on Thursday, Nov. 13, 2025. Michael Nagle | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesThe Commodity Futures Trading Commission is investigating whether prediction market platform Polymarket violated a 2022 settlement meant to ban U.S. users from its offshore platform, according to a person familiar with the matter.The investigation is part of a broader probe the agency opened into Polymarket earlier this year, after a  Wall Street Journal expose said Polymarket paid content creators to post videos showing simulated trades and fabricated wins on dummy versions of its website. The latest inquiry focuses on whether Polymarket previously broke the 2022 settlement, and is unrelated to the platform's present operations, said the person, who spoke on condition of anonymity because they are not authorized to speak publicly.The federal agency is inquiring into Polymarket controls that are meant to detect where customers are located, as well as the platform's advertising in the U.S., the person added.The CFTC is also looking into the company's U.S. platform that launched in late December, specifically in its customer onboarding processes and protection measures, according to the source. Reuters first reported the latest investigation.The person familiar with the inquiry did not provide a start date for when the CFTC began investigating Polymarket. News of the CFTC probe comes one week before the Nov. 3 midterm elections, with polls showing Democrats leading to take control of the House of Representatives from Republicans, and a neck and neck race for the Senate, amid escalating concern from mental health experts and lawmakers about prediction markets' explosive growth in the past year. Polymarket declined to comment on the investigation. The CFTC did not respond to a request for comment. In 2022, Polymarket stopped U.S. users from accessing its platform and paid a $1.4 million civil penalty to the CFTC as part of an enforcement settlement with the agency during the Biden administration. In 2024, the CFTC opened a probe into whether Polymarket was complying with that agreement, and the Justice Department opened a related investigation. Both federal agencies closed those investigations into the platform in July 2025. Disclosure: CNBC and Kalshi have a commercial relationship that includes customer acquisition and a minority investment.

schema.headline: Polymarket faces renewed CFTC probe over U.S. access to offshore platform

title: Neil Young sues Trump committee for $10M for playing 'Rockin' in the Free World' at rally
description: Neil Young performs as part of a historic double bill with Bob Dylan at Hyde Park on July 12, 2019 in London, England. Dave J Hogan | Getty ImagesLege
body: Neil Young performs as part of a historic double bill with Bob Dylan at Hyde Park on July 12, 2019 in London, England. Dave J Hogan | Getty ImagesLegendary musician Neil Young filed a $10 million lawsuit against President Donald Trump's campaign committee for infringing Young's copyright by playing his song "Rockin' in the Free World" just before the president took the stage to speak at an Oct. 12  rally in Youngstown, Ohio.The Trump 47 Committee has caused that song, without the musician's permission, "to be played numerous times at other rallies designed to encourage Republican votes in the upcoming mid-term elections," Young's lawsuit in U.S. District Court in Richmond, Virginia, alleges.Trump "was personally aware that a license would be required to play the Song at rallies," and that Young "has not, and would not, grant the required license," the suit filed Monday says.Young, 80, in 2020 sued another corporation formed by Trump, Donald J. Trump for President Inc., in Manhattan federal court for copyright infringement of "Rockin' in the Free World,"  and another song written by Young, "Devil's Sidewalk," for having played the songs without permission at campaign rallies.In that first case, Trump's corporation "asserted no defense and immediately settled shortly after it was served, promising that it would never again use 'Rockin' in the Free World' without a license and permission from Young," the new suit said.CNBC has requested comment from the Trump 47 Committee about the suit, and from Young's lawyers.The White House, when asked for comment, referred CNBC to the Republican National Committee, which did not immediately respond to an email seeking comment.Young, who was born in Canada, is a naturalized U.S. citizen. He is a two-time inductee in the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame: in 1995 as a solo artist, and in 1997 as a member of Buffalo Springfield. Young was also a member of the folk rock supergroup Crosby, Stills, Nash & Young.Young released "Rockin' in the Free World" in 1989.His lawsuit describes the tune as a "blistering anthem that contrasts the hollow promises of American political rhetoric with the harsh realities faced by the poor, homeless and forgotten."The lyrics include descriptions of a mother discarding her baby, addiction, and "garbage piling in the shadows of prosperity — while the repeated chorus delivers savage irony, celebrating freedom that clearly isn't shared by all," the suit notes."In short, the Song is the opposite of everything that Donald J. Trump stands for," the suit says.In addition to the Trump 47 Committee, the suit lists five other defendants, identified by the pseudonym "Doe," whom Young believes are liable for infringing on Young's copyright.The Oct. 12 Trump rally that is referenced in the lawsuit was also the scene of an incident that has drawn attention from local law enforcement. Videos from the rally show several attendees apparently attacking and beating a woman, Blake Miley, who had repeatedly yelled 'fascist" at Trump while wearing a shirt bearing the message "Release the Epstein Files."Mahoning County, Ohio, Sheriff Jerry Greene reportedly is investigating three individuals in connection with the incident.

schema.headline: Neil Young sues Trump committee for $10M for playing 'Rockin' in the Free World' at rally

title: One week out, prediction markets see Democrats as favored to sweep Congress
description: The U.S. Capitol building is seen on March 27, 2026 in Washington, DC.Samuel Corum | Getty ImagesThe 2026 U.S. midterm election will be held a week fr
body: The U.S. Capitol building is seen on March 27, 2026 in Washington, DC.Samuel Corum | Getty ImagesThe 2026 U.S. midterm election will be held a week from Tuesday, with the Republican Party looking to defend majorities in both the House and Senate, though Democrats are seen as two-to-one favorites to flip both chambers blue on prediction markets. Speculators on platform Kalshi place a 63% chance that Democrats win control of both the House and Senate. Those odds have stayed relatively stable since the beginning of October. Meanwhile, there's just under a 10% chance that Republicans sweep both chambers, and a 29% chance Democrats win the House while the GOP maintains its majority in the Senate. Contracts on the market are resolved using official data from the U.S. Congress. Odds and gambling platforms do not use methodologies used by traditional political polling, and therefore are not substitutes for political polls.On Sunday, prediction markets gave high odds to right-wing candidate Flavio Bolsonaro to win in the Brazil presidential election before polls closed, though the incumbent left-wing president Lula da Silva was re-elected. Some markets in Democratic primaries this election cycle also drew criticism for giving sky-high odds to some candidates winning who ultimately only narrowly won or lost. Platforms, however, say that odds traders place often end up happening that exact percentage of the time. That means, essentially, that a candidate with a 20% chance to win on an event contract exchange pulls out an "upset" win 20% of the time. Before early September, Democrats had less than a 50% chance to sweep both chambers of Congress, though their odds have risen from around 30% earlier in the year before the start of the U.S.-Iran war and higher gas prices that have hit consumers. On Polymarket, Democrats have a 65% chance to sweep both houses. Polls broadly show Democrats favored in the national popular vote for the House, and competitive in a series of red-state Senate races that will decide control of the upper chamber. Though House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., has cast doubt on those findings. "We've been from coast to coast," he said in an appearance on Fox News Monday, "and I'm telling you, the polling is inaccurate."Disclosure: CNBC and Kalshi have a commercial relationship that includes customer acquisition and a minority investment.

schema.headline: One week out, prediction markets see Democrats as favored to sweep Congress

title: Trump administration may let more Russian diesel onto market, energy secretary tells CNBC
description: watch nowThe U.S. may allow more diesel fuel from Russia onto the global market depending on Moscow's behavior, Energy Secretary Chris Wright told CNB
body: watch nowThe U.S. may allow more diesel fuel from Russia onto the global market depending on Moscow's behavior, Energy Secretary Chris Wright told CNBC in an interview Tuesday. Wright framed the Trump administration's suspension of U.S. sanctions against Russian diesel exports earlier this month as "an incentive" for Moscow to end the war in Ukraine. It will help with fuel supplies on the margin, he said.The Russian-flagged tanker Talisman is expected to arrive on the U.S. East Coast on Nov. 9, according to the ship-tracking platform MarineTraffic. Another tanker, the Leruo, has departed Russia en route to the "Atlantic Coast" without explicitly declaring its destination as the U.S. More tankers with Russian diesel could "quite possibly" set sail under the U.S. sanctions waiver, Wright told CNBC's "Power Lunch." "It's trying to put a carrot in front of Russia," the energy secretary said. President Donald Trump struck a deal with President Vladimir Putin for Russia to export 800,000 metric tons of diesel in October and November, followed by another million tons. Trump reached the agreement with Putin as he faces political pressure to reduce surging diesel prices ahead of the U.S. midterm elections next Tuesday. Fuel prices have spiked since the U.S. and Israel attacked Iran on Feb. 28. But the diesel volumes in the Trump-Putin deal won't materially lower prices because the shipments are small compared with total global demand of around 28 million barrels per day, analysts say. The first shipment from Russia of 300,000 metric tons is equivalent to about 75,000 barrels per day if rolled out over one month. The second tranche, of 500,000 metric tons, equals about 124,000 bpd.Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has sharply criticized the diesel deal. Kyiv has pounded Russian refineries this year in an effort to cut the revenue the Kremlin collects from energy exports and curtail Moscow's ability to wage war. The strikes forced Moscow to implement a diesel export ban in July. The Kremlin has partially lifted that ban to fulfill the Trump-Putin deal. Several Republican senators also slammed the deal, signing a letter with Democratic colleagues that condemned the agreement as "a gift to our adversary and a betrayal of our Allies."

schema.headline: Trump administration may let more Russian diesel onto market, energy secretary tells CNBC

title: JetBlue stock surges as company outlook calms investors
description: JetBlue planes populate the tarmac on June 24, 2026 at JFK Airport in the Queens borough of New York City.  Bruce Bennett | Getty ImagesJetBlue Airway
body: JetBlue planes populate the tarmac on June 24, 2026 at JFK Airport in the Queens borough of New York City.  Bruce Bennett | Getty ImagesJetBlue Airways reported a bigger loss in the third quarter compared with last year, but shares surged as the carrier's upbeat forecast that it will return to profitability appeared to calm investors after a Monday rout.JetBlue stock rose 18% in trading Tuesday after hitting a new low a day earlier as investors fretted about the company's financial future.The Monday drop came after the Wall Street Journal reported Friday that a group of the airline's senior creditors is reportedly working with restructuring adviser PJT Partners."We have no intention, no plans to file for bankruptcy. We are not engaged with any restructuring company," CEO Joanna Geraghty told CNBC on Tuesday. "We are focused on delivering to our shareholders what we laid out for at the beginning of our turnaround plan."She said there is a "fundamental disconnect between the narrative in the bond market and what our financial results actually demonstrate."The New York airline late Monday reported that its revenue per available seat mile, a key metric measuring how much operating revenue a carrier generates for every seat flown one mile, would be up as much as 22% in the fourth quarter, bringing the annual increase to an expected 13.5% to 14.5%"We're not seeing any meaningful pushback," Geraghty said in the interview.Read more about airlines' race to win over big spendersAlaska Airlines unveils massive premium cabin overhaul in high-end travel raceBudget airline king Bill Franke warms to first-class seats and premium upgradesUnited ditches more economy seats to make room for bigger premium cabins with new layoutsCaviar and privacy: Airlines' business-class wars are hereAmerican Airlines is arriving late to the luxury travel boom. Can it catch up?First-class seats are getting so fancy they’re holding up new airplanesAirlines can’t add high-end seats fast enough as travelers treat themselves to first classJetBlue on Monday posted a net loss of $257 million for the three months ended Sept. 30, compared with a loss of $143 million a year earlier. The carrier's fuel bill rose 61% to $868 million. The carrier said it ended the quarter with $2.2 billion in liquidity and that its unencumbered asset base is now $7 billion, including $2.8 billion in aircraft and engines.JetBlue had total debt of $8.4 billion as of Sept. 30, the carrier said in its earnings filing Monday."Importantly, we believe we have the liquidity and financing options to create a strong bridge to at least $1 EPS and positive free cash flow in 2028," CFO Ursula Hurley said in a statement. "We remain focused on disciplined cost execution and capital management as we work toward sustained profitability and positive free cash flow."Here is what JetBlue reported in the third quarter compared with Wall Street estimates compiled by LSEG:Loss per share: 60 cents adjusted vs. a loss of 55 cents expectedRevenue: $2.81 billion vs. $2.82 billion expectedJetBlue last posted an annual profit in 2019. The airline is in the middle of a multiyear turnaround plan that includes cutting cuts and boosting revenue by investing in premium seats, like a new domestic first class section that recently went on sale.Fuel costs have eaten into airline profits across the board. JetBlue said travel demand has remained strong despite higher fares.JetBlue's average fares rose more than 19% to $245.11 in the third quarter from $205.67 in the year-earlier period.The airline has struggled not just with higher costs but also with competition from larger rivals. It sought to acquire now-defunct carrier Spirit Airlines, but that deal was upended by a federal judge who ruled it was anticompetitive. A judge also blocked a regional partnership between JetBlue and American Airlines, which the airlines argued would help them compete better against carriers in the congested Northeast U.S. JetBlue now has a partnership with United Airlines. The carrier expects to grow capacity no more than 4% in the current quarter. One bright spot, executives said, has been expanding at Fort Lauderdale-Hollywood International Airport, the former home hub of Spirit, which collapsed in May.

schema.headline: JetBlue stock surges as company outlook calms investors
